title: Eyes, Ears, Nose & Throat
summary: The head's sensory organs and airway entrance, from the red eye and sudden vision loss to earache, epistaxis, sore throat and neck masses. Focus is recognition: mechanism, the can't-miss presentation, and the first action.

lessons.title: Inside the eye and the exam that reads it
lessons.body:
## The eye as a camera

Light passes through a clear dome at the front (the **cornea**), through a hole whose size the colored iris controls (the **pupil**), through a focusing lens, across a jelly-filled chamber (the **vitreous**), and lands on a sheet of light-sensing tissue at the back (the **retina**). The retina turns light into nerve signals and sends them down the optic nerve to the brain.

Two fluid facts matter. The front chamber is filled with a watery fluid (**aqueous humor**) that is made continuously and drains through a mesh at the angle where the iris meets the cornea. If drainage stops, pressure climbs and the eye hurts. The back chamber's jelly is made once in life and never replaced, so when it shrinks with age it can tug the retina loose.

## The seven-part eye exam

Every eye complaint gets the same sequence, and the order is not arbitrary.

1. **Visual acuity** — the vital sign of the eye. Measure each eye separately, with the patient's glasses on. `20/40` means they see at 20 feet what a normal eye sees at 40. Document it before you touch anything.
2. **Pupils** — size, equality, reaction to light. Normal is `2-4 mm` in light, briskly constricting.
3. **Extraocular movements (EOM)** — track an H pattern. Pain or restriction points to muscle entrapment, nerve palsy, or orbital infection.
4. **Visual fields** — confrontation, one quadrant at a time. A missing quadrant or half is a retinal or brain problem, not a refraction problem.
5. **Fundoscopy** — look through the pupil at the retina, the optic disc, and the vessels.
6. **Intraocular pressure (IOP)** — normal `10-21 mmHg`. Above `21` is abnormal; above `40` with pain is an emergency.
7. **Fluorescein** — orange dye plus a blue light. Damaged cornea holds the dye and glows green.

## The swinging flashlight test

Swing a light from one eye to the other every 2-3 seconds. Normally both pupils stay constricted. If one pupil *dilates* when the light reaches it, that eye is sending a weaker signal to the brain — a **relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD)**, also called a Marcus Gunn pupil.

An RAPD means the problem is in the retina or optic nerve, not in the lens or cornea. Cataracts, corneal scars and refractive error never cause it.

> **Key:** Visual acuity is the eye's vital sign. An eye complaint charted without an acuity is an incomplete exam.

## Two shortcuts that separate causes

If blurred vision sharpens when the patient looks through a pinhole, the problem is refractive or in the media, not the retina or nerve. If pressing lightly through a closed lid feels rock-hard compared with the other eye, suspect very high pressure.

> **Trap:** Never measure pressure, never press on the globe, and never instill dye if you suspect the eyeball is ruptured. Pressure can push the contents out.

Topical anesthetic drops (`proparacaine 0.5%`) are for the exam only. They slow corneal healing, so patients never go home with them.
keyPoints: Visual acuity is the eye's vital sign and is documented before anything else, each eye separately.
Normal intraocular pressure is 10-21 mmHg; over 21 is abnormal, over 40 with pain is an emergency.
An RAPD (swinging flashlight, pupil dilates to light) localizes the problem to retina or optic nerve.
Fluorescein plus blue light shows corneal defects as green; skip it if globe rupture is suspected.
Pinhole improvement means a refractive or media problem, not a retina or nerve problem.

checks.q: A patient with a painful red eye has light swung between the eyes. The left pupil dilates each time the light reaches it. What does this indicate?
choices: A defect in the left retina or optic nerve
A cataract in the left lens
checks.why: A pupil that dilates to direct light is a relative afferent pupillary defect, meaning that eye transmits a weaker signal. Cataracts and corneal injuries block light but do not produce an RAPD.

checks.q: Which finding is outside the normal range?
checks.why: Normal IOP is 10-21 mmHg, so 34 is clearly elevated. The other three findings are all normal.

checks.q: Why are topical anesthetic drops not sent home with a patient?
choices: They delay corneal healing and mask worsening injury
checks.why: Proparacaine slows epithelial healing and removes the pain that would otherwise signal a worsening ulcer. It does not raise pressure or dilate the pupil; fluorescein, not anesthetic, stains lenses.

lessons.title: Red eye: sorting the harmless from the sight-threatening
lessons.body:
## Three questions do most of the sorting

A red eye is a symptom, not a diagnosis. Ask: is vision affected, is there real pain (not just itch or grit), and where is the redness concentrated?

Redness spread across the whole white with normal vision and no true pain is almost always surface irritation. Redness gathered in a ring right around the cornea (**ciliary flush**) with aching pain and reduced vision means the problem is inside the eye.

## Conjunctivitis: the common three

The conjunctiva is the clear film over the white of the eye. Inflame it and vessels dilate.

| Type | Discharge | Clues |
|---|---|---|
| Viral | Watery | Usually adenovirus, starts one eye then the other, tender node in front of the ear, recent cold |
| Bacterial | Thick yellow-green, lids stuck shut on waking | Often one eye, responds to topical antibiotic |
| Allergic | Stringy, clear | Both eyes, itching is the dominant symptom, seasonal |

Itching points to allergy. Gluing shut overnight points to bacteria. Viral conjunctivitis is intensely contagious for `10-14 days` and is managed with hygiene and cool compresses, not antibiotics.

> **Trap:** Copious thick pus appearing `12-24 hours` after exposure in a sexually active adult or a newborn is gonococcal conjunctivitis. It can eat through the cornea in a day and needs systemic treatment, not eye drops alone.

## The dangerous four

**Keratitis** is inflammation of the cornea itself. Pain, light sensitivity (**photophobia**), tearing, and a cornea that is no longer crystal clear. A branching, fern-like pattern on fluorescein is herpes simplex — never give steroid drops for that, they can perforate the cornea.

**Uveitis or iritis** is inflammation inside the front chamber. Deep aching pain, photophobia so strong that light in the *other* eye hurts the affected one (consensual photophobia), ciliary flush, a small sluggish pupil, and cells floating in the chamber on slit lamp. It travels with autoimmune disease, especially ankylosing spondylitis and inflammatory bowel disease.

**Acute angle-closure glaucoma** is drainage blocked suddenly. Severe pain, nausea and vomiting, halos around lights, a hazy cornea, and a mid-dilated pupil that barely reacts. IOP is often `40-70 mmHg`. It classically starts in a dark room or after a pupil-dilating drug. This is an hours-matter emergency.

**Scleritis** is inflammation of the tough white wall. The pain is boring, deep, wakes the patient at night, and the redness has a violet cast that does not blanch with a vasoconstrictor drop. Half of cases sit on top of rheumatoid arthritis or vasculitis. **Episcleritis** looks similar but is painless or mildly uncomfortable, blanches with phenylephrine, and resolves on its own.

## Contact lenses change everything

A contact lens wearer with a red painful eye is assumed to have a corneal ulcer until proven otherwise, often *Pseudomonas*. Lenses come out, no patching (a patch incubates the bacteria), and they need same-day ophthalmology.

> **Key:** Pain plus vision loss plus ciliary flush is never simple conjunctivitis. That triad buys an urgent eye evaluation.
keyPoints: Diffuse redness with normal vision and no pain is surface disease; ciliary flush with pain and vision loss is intraocular.
Itching means allergic, morning crusting means bacterial, watery with a preauricular node means viral.
Acute angle-closure glaucoma: severe pain, vomiting, halos, hazy cornea, mid-dilated fixed pupil, IOP 40-70 mmHg.
Dendritic fluorescein staining is herpes keratitis; steroid drops are contraindicated.
Contact lens wearer with a red painful eye equals corneal ulcer until proven otherwise, and never patch it.

checks.q: A 58-year-old comes from a dim movie theater with severe right eye pain, vomiting, halos around lights, and a mid-dilated pupil. What is the most likely diagnosis?
checks.why: Dim light dilates the pupil and can block the drainage angle, spiking pressure. Vomiting, halos and a mid-dilated fixed pupil are classic. Conjunctivitis does not cause halos or vomiting, and episcleritis is not severely painful.

checks.q: Fluorescein staining shows a branching dendritic pattern on the cornea. Which treatment must be avoided?
checks.why: A dendrite means herpes simplex keratitis. Steroids suppress local immunity and can drive the ulcer deeper to perforation. Antivirals and referral are the correct path.

lessons.title: Sudden vision loss: the six that cannot wait
lessons.body:
## Frame it by pain and by pattern

Sudden loss of vision splits cleanly. Painless loss is almost always vascular or retinal. Painful loss points to the optic nerve or the front of the eye. Then ask whether it is the whole field, half the field, or a curtain over part of it.

## Painless

**Retinal detachment.** The retina peels off the wall it feeds from. The patient describes a sudden shower of floaters, flashes of light (**photopsia**), then a dark curtain moving across the field. It is painless. Risk rises with nearsightedness, prior cataract surgery, and age. Treatment is surgical, and the urgency is whether the central vision area (**macula**) is still attached — a macula-on detachment is a same-day repair.

**Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO).** A clot or cholesterol plug blocks the artery feeding the retina. Vision goes in seconds, painlessly, and is profound — often counting fingers or worse. There is an RAPD. The fundus is pale with a **cherry-red spot** at the macula. This is a stroke of the eye: retinal tissue starts dying in about `90 minutes`, and these patients go down a stroke pathway.

**Central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO).** The drainage vein clots instead. Loss is usually less abrupt and less total. The fundus looks like **blood and thunder** — hemorrhages scattered in every quadrant with a swollen disc. It rides on hypertension, diabetes, glaucoma and hyperviscosity.

**Vitreous hemorrhage.** Blood leaks into the jelly, usually from fragile new vessels in diabetic retinopathy. Sudden floaters, cobwebs, or a red haze, painless, with a fundus you cannot see through.

**Amaurosis fugax.** Painless vision loss in one eye lasting `2-30 minutes`, described as a shade pulled down and then lifted. It is a transient ischemic attack of the eye, usually from carotid plaque. Full recovery does not make it benign — it predicts stroke and earns a carotid workup.

## Painful

**Giant cell arteritis (GCA).** Inflammation of medium arteries in the head in patients over `50`, most over `70`. Headache at the temple, scalp tenderness, jaw pain while chewing (**jaw claudication**), and often shoulder-hip stiffness from polymyalgia rheumatica. ESR and CRP are high. Vision loss can be sudden and permanent, and the second eye follows within days if untreated. **High-dose steroids start before the biopsy.**

**Optic neuritis.** Inflammation of the optic nerve, typically a woman aged `20-40`. Vision dims over hours to days, colors look washed out (red looks faded), and the eye aches with movement. There is an RAPD. Roughly half go on to develop multiple sclerosis, so it earns an MRI.

> **Key:** Painless, sudden, total, with a cherry-red spot equals CRAO. Treat it with stroke-level urgency, not an eye-clinic appointment next week.

> **On shift:** Any patient over 50 with a new temporal headache and any visual symptom gets an ESR and CRP drawn early. That single lab pair changes the disposition.
keyPoints: Flashes, floaters, then a curtain equals retinal detachment; urgency depends on whether the macula is still attached.
CRAO is painless, profound, has an RAPD and a cherry-red spot; retinal damage begins around 90 minutes.
CRVO shows blood-and-thunder fundus hemorrhages in all four quadrants with a swollen disc.
GCA in a patient over 50 with temporal headache and jaw claudication gets steroids before biopsy.
Amaurosis fugax lasting 2-30 minutes with full recovery is a TIA of the eye and needs a carotid workup.

checks.q: A 72-year-old reports a new left temporal headache, scalp tenderness, and pain in the jaw while chewing. Vision in the left eye blurred this morning. What is the first action?
choices: Schedule a temporal artery biopsy for next week and observe
Prescribe ibuprofen and follow up in 48 hours
Start high-dose corticosteroids now and arrange biopsy
Order a CT of the orbits before any treatment
checks.why: Giant cell arteritis can blind the second eye within days. Steroids are started immediately; the biopsy remains positive for a week or more afterward, so treatment is not delayed for it.

checks.q: Which presentation best fits central retinal artery occlusion?
choices: Painless, seconds-long onset of profound loss with a cherry-red macular spot and RAPD
Gradual dimming over days with pain on eye movement and washed-out colors
Flashes and floaters followed by a curtain across the lower field
Deep aching pain with halos and a hazy cornea
checks.why: CRAO is instantaneous, painless and severe with a pale retina and cherry-red spot. The second describes optic neuritis, the third retinal detachment, the fourth angle-closure glaucoma.

checks.q: A diabetic patient reports sudden floaters and a red haze in one eye, painless, and the retina cannot be visualized. What is most likely?
checks.why: Fragile new vessels from diabetic retinopathy bleed into the vitreous, producing floaters, haze and an obscured fundus. Optic neuritis is painful with movement, and amaurosis fugax resolves within 30 minutes.

lessons.title: Eye trauma from grit to globe rupture
lessons.body:
## Chemicals come before everything

A chemical splash is the only eye complaint that is treated before the history is taken and before acuity is measured. Alkali (drain cleaner, lye, cement, oven cleaner) dissolves cell membranes and keeps burrowing inward. Acid coagulates protein and tends to stop itself, so alkali is worse.

Irrigate immediately with at least `1-2 liters` of normal saline or lactated Ringer's per eye, running `15-30 minutes`. Then wait `5 minutes` after stopping and check the tear film pH with litmus paper. Target is `pH 7.0-7.4`. If it is still off, keep irrigating. Anesthetic drops and a lid speculum make this tolerable, and the upper lid must be everted to sweep out cement or lime particles.

> **Key:** Chemical burn means irrigate first, ask questions second, and stop only when the pH sits at 7.0-7.4 on recheck.

## Corneal abrasion and foreign body

A scratch on the cornea produces intense pain, tearing, a foreign-body sensation and photophobia. Fluorescein shows a green defect. Treat with lubrication and an antibiotic ointment, oral analgesia, and no patching. Contact lens wearers get a `Pseudomonas`-covering drop such as a fluoroquinolone.

Vertical linear scratches mean something is still stuck under the upper lid — evert it and look. Metal on a cornea leaves a rust ring that needs removal within `24 hours`.

> **Trap:** High-speed grinding, hammering metal on metal, or a weed trimmer are the histories that hide an intraocular foreign body. A pain-free eye with good acuity after hammering still earns imaging, and CT beats plain film. Never MRI a possible metal fragment.

## Hyphema

Blood pools in the front chamber and settles into a visible horizontal line. It follows blunt trauma, hurts, and blurs vision. Keep the head elevated `30-45 degrees` so blood settles away from the visual axis, shield the eye, avoid aspirin and NSAIDs, and check IOP. The danger is rebleeding on days `3-5` and pressure spikes. Sickle cell trait or disease makes even a small hyphema high-risk.

## Orbital blowout fracture

A fist or ball larger than the orbital rim transmits pressure to the thin floor, which cracks downward into the maxillary sinus. The result is pain with upward gaze, double vision (**diplopia**) when the inferior rectus is trapped, numbness of the cheek and upper lip from infraorbital nerve injury, and sometimes a sunken-looking eye. CT of the orbits confirms it. Tell the patient not to blow the nose — it forces sinus air into the orbit.

In children the bone is springy and snaps back, trapping muscle tightly (**white-eyed blowout**). They may look deceptively normal but vomit and have a slow heart rate from vagal stimulation. That is a surgical emergency within `24-48 hours`.

## Globe rupture

Full-thickness breach of the eye wall. Look for a teardrop or irregular pupil, a very soft eye, dark tissue visible at the wound, a deep chamber gone shallow, or a positive **Seidel sign** where fluorescein is diluted by leaking aqueous.

Stop the exam. No pressure measurement, no lid retraction, no further drops. Place a rigid shield, not a pad, elevate the head, treat pain and nausea aggressively so the patient does not strain, give IV antibiotics and tetanus, keep them nothing by mouth, and call ophthalmology.
keyPoints: Chemical burn: irrigate 15-30 minutes with 1-2 L, recheck pH 5 minutes after stopping, target 7.0-7.4; alkali is worse than acid.
Corneal abrasions are not patched; contact lens wearers need Pseudomonas coverage.
Hyphema: head up 30-45 degrees, rigid shield, no NSAIDs, watch for rebleed on days 3-5.
Blowout fracture: pain on upward gaze, diplopia, cheek numbness; children with entrapment plus vomiting and bradycardia need surgery within 24-48 hours.
Suspected globe rupture: rigid shield, stop the exam, no pressure on the eye, IV antibiotics and ophthalmology.

checks.q: A worker splashes lye in one eye. Which action comes first?
choices: Measure visual acuity in both eyes
Obtain a CT of the orbits
Begin continuous irrigation with normal saline
Instill fluorescein and examine with a blue light
checks.why: Alkali keeps penetrating tissue every second it stays in contact, so irrigation precedes acuity, imaging and staining. Everything else waits until the pH is 7.0-7.4.

checks.q: A 9-year-old was hit in the eye by a ball. He is vomiting, his heart rate is 48, and he cannot look up with that eye. What does this suggest?
choices: Entrapped inferior rectus in a pediatric blowout fracture
checks.why: A trapdoor fracture pinches the muscle and stimulates the vagus, producing nausea, vomiting and bradycardia with restricted upgaze. This needs surgical release within 24-48 hours.

checks.q: Which finding most strongly suggests a ruptured globe?
choices: Bright green staining of a linear corneal scratch
Diffuse redness with thick yellow discharge
A blood level in the anterior chamber
A teardrop-shaped pupil with a soft eye and positive Seidel sign
checks.why: An irregular teardrop pupil, low pressure and aqueous streaming through dye are the hallmarks of a full-thickness breach. Abrasions, conjunctivitis and hyphema do not deform the pupil this way.

lessons.title: The ear: from canal to mastoid
lessons.body:
## Three compartments

The **outer ear** is the visible pinna and the canal, ending at the eardrum (**tympanic membrane**). The **middle ear** is an air pocket behind the drum holding three tiny bones that carry vibration, ventilated by the eustachian tube that runs down to the back of the nose. The **inner ear** is the cochlea for hearing and the semicircular canals for balance.

That eustachian tube explains most childhood ear disease. In a child it is short, floppy and nearly horizontal, so nasal secretions track into the middle ear easily and drain badly. By adolescence it angles downward and infections drop off.

## Otitis externa

Infection of the canal skin, usually `Pseudomonas` or `Staph aureus`, after water exposure or aggressive cleaning. Swimmer's ear.

The giveaway is pain when the pinna is pulled or the tragus is pressed — the canal itself is the tender structure. The canal looks swollen, wet and debris-filled; the drum is usually normal if you can see it. Treat with topical drops such as ofloxacin or neomycin-polymyxin-hydrocortisone for `7-10 days`, keep the ear dry, and place a wick if the canal is too swollen for drops to pass.

> **Trap:** An older diabetic or immunocompromised patient with severe ear pain out of proportion, drainage, and granulation tissue at the bone-cartilage junction has **malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa** — the infection has reached bone. That is IV antibiotics and imaging, not drops.

## Otitis media

Fluid and bacteria trapped behind the drum, usually after a cold. The top organisms are `Strep pneumoniae`, `Haemophilus influenzae` and `Moraxella catarrhalis`.

Diagnosis requires a **bulging** drum plus signs of acute illness, not just redness — a crying child has a red drum. Look for bulging, loss of landmarks, and reduced mobility on pneumatic otoscopy. Pulling on the pinna does not hurt, which separates it from otitis externa.

First-line treatment is high-dose amoxicillin `80-90 mg/kg/day` divided twice daily, or amoxicillin-clavulanate if there was an antibiotic in the last `30 days`. Watchful waiting for `48-72 hours` with analgesia is reasonable in a child over `2` with mild unilateral disease and reliable follow-up.

**Otitis media with effusion** is fluid without infection — a dull, retracted drum, hearing muffled, no fever and no pain. It needs no antibiotics, but persistent effusion beyond `3 months` with hearing loss earns ENT referral and possibly tubes.

## Cerumen, perforation, and two complications

Cerumen impaction causes muffled hearing, fullness and sometimes dizziness. Irrigate with body-temperature water, or soften with carbamide peroxide. Never irrigate if the drum may be perforated or if tubes are in place.

A perforated drum from pressure, a slap, a blast or a cotton swab causes sudden pain that then eases, bleeding and hearing loss. Most heal on their own in `6-8 weeks`. Keep the ear dry and do not irrigate.

**Mastoiditis** is otitis media that eroded into the bone behind the ear. The pinna is pushed out and forward, and the area behind it is red, swollen and tender. It needs CT, IV antibiotics and ENT.

**Cholesteatoma** is a ball of trapped skin cells growing in the middle ear, classically after chronic retraction. Painless, chronically draining, foul-smelling ear with progressive hearing loss. It erodes bone and is surgical.

> **Key:** Tragal tenderness points outward to the canal. A bulging immobile drum points inward to the middle ear.
keyPoints: Pain on tragal pressure or pinna traction means otitis externa; a bulging immobile drum means otitis media.
Acute otitis media first-line is high-dose amoxicillin 80-90 mg/kg/day divided BID; use amoxicillin-clavulanate if antibiotics within 30 days.
Severe pain, drainage and granulation tissue in a diabetic means necrotizing otitis externa and IV therapy.
A pinna pushed out and forward with tenderness behind the ear is mastoiditis until proven otherwise.
Painless, foul, chronically draining ear with worsening hearing suggests cholesteatoma, which is surgical.

checks.q: A 16-year-old swimmer has ear pain that worsens sharply when the tragus is pressed. The canal is swollen and full of debris. What is the diagnosis?
checks.why: Tragal tenderness localizes inflammation to the canal skin. Otitis media does not hurt with pinna manipulation, mastoiditis pushes the pinna outward, and cholesteatoma is painless.

checks.q: Which finding is required to diagnose acute otitis media rather than simply a red drum?
choices: Any redness of the tympanic membrane
Pain when the pinna is pulled
A bulging tympanic membrane with reduced mobility
checks.why: Redness alone appears with crying or fever. Bulging with loss of landmarks and poor mobility on pneumatic otoscopy is the defining finding. Pinna pain points to the canal instead.

lessons.title: Hearing loss and the dizzy patient
lessons.body:
## Two kinds of deafness

Sound has to be conducted through the canal, drum and bones, then sensed by the cochlea and carried by the nerve. Block the first path and you have **conductive** loss — wax, fluid, perforation, otosclerosis. Damage the second and you have **sensorineural** loss — noise, aging, drugs, tumors.

**Weber**: strike a `512 Hz` tuning fork and place it on the middle of the forehead. Normally sound is heard equally. It lateralizes *toward* a conductive loss (that ear is shielded from room noise, so the bone-conducted tone seems louder) and *away from* a sensorineural loss.

**Rinne**: compare the fork held next to the ear (air) with the fork on the mastoid bone (bone). Normal and sensorineural ears hear air longer than bone, which is a positive Rinne. Conductive loss reverses it — bone beats air.

| Pattern | Weber | Rinne |
|---|---|---|
| Normal | Midline | Air > bone both ears |
| Conductive right | Lateralizes right | Bone > air on the right |
| Sensorineural right | Lateralizes left | Air > bone both ears |

**Presbycusis** is age-related sensorineural loss that takes high frequencies first, which is why consonants blur and restaurants become impossible while the patient insists people mumble.

> **Key:** Sudden sensorineural hearing loss in one ear over `72 hours` or less is an emergency. High-dose oral steroids started within `2 weeks` (ideally within days) is the only chance at recovery, so it is not a routine ENT referral.

## Vertigo means the room spins

Dizziness is a useless word. Vertigo is a false sense of motion, and it means the balance organs or their brain connections. The first fork in the road is peripheral (inner ear, common, benign) versus central (brainstem or cerebellum, rare, dangerous).

**BPPV.** Loose calcium crystals drift into a semicircular canal. Spinning lasts `10-60 seconds`, triggered by rolling over in bed or tipping the head back, no hearing loss, no other neurologic signs. **Dix-Hallpike** reproduces it: sit the patient up, turn the head `45 degrees`, lay them back quickly with the head extended `20 degrees` below the table, and watch for a few seconds of delay then rotary nystagmus that fatigues. The **Epley maneuver** rolls the crystals back out and works in most patients in one or two sessions.

**Vestibular neuritis.** Inflammation of the balance nerve, usually after a viral illness. Constant severe vertigo lasting `days`, worse with movement, nausea and vomiting, normal hearing. If hearing is also lost it is called labyrinthitis.

**Meniere disease.** Too much fluid pressure in the inner ear. Attacks of `20 minutes to 12 hours` with the full triad: vertigo, fluctuating low-frequency hearing loss, ear fullness, and roaring tinnitus. Managed with salt restriction under `2 g/day` and diuretics.

**Central causes.** Stroke of the cerebellum or brainstem, vestibular migraine, MS plaque, tumor. Red flags are new severe headache, double vision, slurred speech, numbness, weakness, inability to walk unassisted, and nystagmus that changes direction with gaze or is purely vertical.

## HINTS, at recognition level

In a patient with continuous vertigo and nystagmus right now, three bedside findings sort peripheral from central. A **normal** head-impulse test, **direction-changing** nystagmus, or a **skew** deviation on cover-uncover each point *central*. Ironically the reassuring-sounding normal head impulse is the worrying one, because a real inner-ear injury should produce a catch-up saccade.

> **Trap:** A patient who cannot stand or walk without falling is central until imaging says otherwise, no matter how convincing the inner-ear story sounds.
keyPoints: Weber lateralizes toward conductive loss and away from sensorineural; conductive loss reverses Rinne so bone beats air.
Sudden sensorineural hearing loss is an emergency treated with high-dose steroids, ideally within days and no later than 2 weeks.
BPPV spins for 10-60 seconds with position change, is diagnosed by Dix-Hallpike and treated by Epley.
Meniere is the triad of episodic vertigo lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours, fluctuating hearing loss, and ear fullness with tinnitus.
Normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus, or skew deviation each point to a central cause.

checks.q: A patient has spinning that lasts about 30 seconds every time she rolls over in bed, with normal hearing and a normal neuro exam. Which test confirms it?
checks.why: Brief positional vertigo is BPPV, reproduced by Dix-Hallpike. Weber and Rinne assess hearing pathways, and Romberg tests proprioception rather than canal function.

checks.q: Weber lateralizes to the left ear and Rinne shows bone conduction longer than air on the left. What kind of loss is this?
checks.why: Lateralization toward the affected ear plus a reversed Rinne on that side is the conductive pattern. Sensorineural loss lateralizes away and keeps air greater than bone.

checks.q: Which feature most strongly suggests a central rather than peripheral cause of continuous vertigo?
choices: Nystagmus that changes direction with gaze
checks.why: Direction-changing nystagmus is a central sign. Nausea, movement sensitivity and tinnitus all occur commonly with peripheral inner-ear disease.

lessons.title: Nose and sinuses: bleeding, blocked and infected
lessons.body:
## Why noses bleed where they do

The front of the nasal septum carries a convergence of five arteries called **Kiesselbach plexus**. It sits on thin cartilage with no fat padding, right where fingers, dry air and forced air from a heater reach it. About `90%` of nosebleeds start there and are called **anterior**.

**Posterior** bleeds come from the sphenopalatine artery further back. They are heavier, often bilateral, run down the throat even when the patient leans forward, and are more common in older hypertensive patients and those on anticoagulants. They can cause real blood loss.

## Stepwise epistaxis management

1. Have the patient blow out clots, then **pinch the soft part of the nose**, not the bony bridge, leaning forward, for `10-15 minutes` uninterrupted. Watching the clock matters more than anything else on this list.
2. Add a vasoconstrictor spray such as oxymetazoline before re-pinching.
3. Look with a speculum and light. If a bleeding point is visible and dry, cauterize with silver nitrate — one side of the septum only, never both, or the septum can die and perforate.
4. If it keeps bleeding, pack anteriorly with an expandable tampon or coated gauze.
5. Bleeding that continues with a good anterior pack, or blood pouring down the throat, means a posterior source: balloon or posterior pack, admit, and call ENT. These patients are monitored, because a posterior pack can disturb breathing.

Check a platelet count and INR if the patient is anticoagulated, and control severe hypertension. Send patients home with saline gel, humidification, and instructions not to pick or blow hard for `1 week`.

> **Key:** Pinch the soft cartilage for a full 10-15 minutes by the clock before escalating. Most failed home attempts are failures of timing and location, not of anatomy.

## Runny, stuffy noses that are not infections

**Allergic rhinitis** is an IgE response to pollen, dust mite or dander. Sneezing, clear discharge, itchy nose and eyes, pale boggy turbinates, and dark circles under the eyes from venous congestion. Intranasal corticosteroids are the most effective single treatment; second-generation antihistamines add relief.

**Vasomotor rhinitis** is nonallergic. Congestion and drip triggered by cold air, strong smells, alcohol or spicy food, with no itching and no eye symptoms. Ipratropium nasal spray helps the drip.

**Rhinitis medicamentosa** is rebound congestion from using a decongestant spray longer than `3 days`. The fix is stopping the spray, not more spray.

## Sinusitis and the antibiotic line

Sinuses drain through narrow openings. Swelling from a cold blocks them and mucus stagnates. The overwhelming majority of acute sinusitis is **viral** and improves by day `7-10`.

Bacterial infection is suspected when one of three patterns is present:

- symptoms lasting `10 days or more` without improvement
- **severe** symptoms from the start: fever `39 C (102 F)` or higher plus purulent discharge for `3-4 consecutive days`
- **double worsening**: a typical cold improves, then fever and facial pain return after `5-6 days`

First-line is amoxicillin-clavulanate for `5-10 days` in adults. Chronic sinusitis is `12 weeks or more` of symptoms and is managed with intranasal steroids, saline irrigation and CT imaging, not repeated antibiotic courses.

> **Trap:** Sinus infection that spreads produces eye and brain complications. Swelling, redness, pain with eye movement, bulging (**proptosis**) or double vision means **orbital cellulitis** — CT and IV antibiotics. Bilateral eye findings with cranial nerve palsies and toxic appearance suggests **cavernous sinus thrombosis**, which is rare and life-threatening.
keyPoints: About 90% of nosebleeds are anterior from Kiesselbach plexus; pinch the soft cartilage 10-15 minutes by the clock.
Cauterize only one side of the septum to avoid perforation; blood running down the throat despite a good anterior pack suggests a posterior bleed.
Bacterial sinusitis is suspected at 10+ days without improvement, severe onset with fever 39 C for 3-4 days, or double worsening.
Intranasal corticosteroids are the most effective single agent for allergic rhinitis; decongestant sprays beyond 3 days cause rebound congestion.
Pain with eye movement, proptosis or diplopia in a patient with sinusitis means orbital cellulitis until CT proves otherwise.

checks.q: A patient's cold improved by day 5, then on day 7 fever and facial pain returned and worsened. What does this pattern indicate?
choices: Normal viral course requiring no change
checks.why: Improvement followed by new fever and pain is the double-worsening pattern, one of the three criteria for suspecting bacterial sinusitis. Allergic and rebound rhinitis do not cause fever.

checks.q: Which epistaxis feature most suggests a posterior source?
choices: Bleeding from one nostril that stops with 10 minutes of pinching
Blood continuing to run down the throat despite a well-placed anterior pack
A visible bleeding point on the anterior septum
Bleeding that began after a dry winter night
checks.why: Persistent posterior drainage despite adequate anterior packing points to the sphenopalatine artery. The other three describe typical anterior Kiesselbach bleeding.

lessons.title: Sore throat: scoring it and spotting the airway threats
lessons.body:
## Most sore throats are viral

About `85-90%` of adult pharyngitis is viral. Cough, hoarseness, runny nose, conjunctivitis and mouth ulcers all point away from strep. Group A `Streptococcus` causes roughly `5-15%` of adult and `20-30%` of pediatric cases, and it matters because untreated it can lead to rheumatic fever.

## Centor and McIsaac

Four Centor criteria, one point each:

1. **Fever** by history or measured
2. **Absence of cough**
3. **Tonsillar exudate** or swelling
4. **Tender anterior cervical nodes**

McIsaac adds age: `+1` if age `3-14`, `0` if `15-44`, `-1` if `45 or older`.

Score `0-1` means no testing and no antibiotics. Score `2-3` means test with a rapid antigen test and treat only if positive; in children a negative rapid test is backed up with culture. Score `4-5` means test, and empiric treatment is reasonable while awaiting results.

Treatment is penicillin V or amoxicillin for `10 days`, or a first-generation cephalosporin or azithromycin for penicillin allergy. Patients are no longer contagious after `12-24 hours` of antibiotics.

> **On the exam:** A teenager with a sore throat, exudate, fever and *cough* is being steered toward a viral cause. Cough is the single most useful negative predictor.

## Mononucleosis

Epstein-Barr virus in an adolescent or young adult. Weeks of fatigue, sore throat with heavy exudate, fever, posterior cervical nodes (not just anterior), and an enlarged spleen in about `50%`. Monospot may be falsely negative in the first week. Treatment is supportive.

Two specifics matter. Giving amoxicillin or ampicillin produces a widespread itchy rash in a large minority of patients with mono, reported in roughly a third to half in modern studies rather than the near-universal rate older texts claim. And splenic rupture, though rare, is why contact sports and heavy lifting stop for at least `3-4 weeks`.

## The abscesses

**Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy).** Pus collects beside a tonsil, usually in a teen or young adult. Severe one-sided throat pain, a muffled hot-potato voice, drooling, trismus (difficulty opening the mouth), a bulging tonsil that pushes the uvula toward the *other* side. Treatment is drainage by needle aspiration or incision plus antibiotics.

**Retropharyngeal abscess.** Pus in the space behind the throat, mostly in children under `6` after pharyngitis or a puncture from a fallen object. Fever, neck stiffness, refusal to move the neck, pain on swallowing, and a child who lies still and extends the neck. Lateral neck film shows widened prevertebral soft tissue; CT confirms. Risk is airway compression and spread into the chest.

## Epiglottitis and Ludwig angina

**Epiglottitis** is infection of the flap that covers the airway during swallowing. Hib vaccination made it rare in children, so today it more often hits adults and unvaccinated kids. The classic picture is rapid onset over hours with the three Ds: **drooling, dysphagia, distress**, plus fever, a muffled voice, and a patient sitting upright leaning forward on their hands (**tripod position**). Stridor is late and ominous.

Do not put a tongue depressor or any instrument in that mouth outside a controlled setting — spasm can close the airway. Keep the patient calm and upright, give oxygen, and get the people who can secure an airway in the room. A lateral neck x-ray may show a **thumbprint sign**, but the patient goes nowhere unattended for it.

**Ludwig angina** is a rapidly spreading infection of the floor of the mouth, almost always from a lower molar. The tongue is pushed up and back, the submandibular area is firm and woody, and the patient drools. Same priority: airway first, then IV antibiotics and drainage.

> **Key:** Drooling plus tripod posture plus a muffled voice is an airway emergency until proven otherwise, whatever the underlying cause.
keyPoints: Centor criteria: fever, no cough, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior nodes; McIsaac adds +1 for age 3-14 and -1 for 45 and older.
Score 0-1 needs no testing; 2-3 test and treat if positive; 4-5 test with reasonable empiric treatment. Penicillin or amoxicillin for 10 days.
Mono: posterior cervical nodes, splenomegaly in half, rash with amoxicillin, no contact sports for 3-4 weeks.
Peritonsillar abscess deviates the uvula away from the swollen side with trismus and a muffled voice; drainage plus antibiotics.
Epiglottitis: drooling, dysphagia, distress, tripod position; do not instrument the airway outside a controlled setting.

checks.q: A 20-year-old has fever, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes, and no cough. What is the McIsaac score and appropriate step?
choices: Score 4; test with rapid antigen and consider empiric treatment
checks.why: All four Centor criteria are present and age 15-44 adds zero, giving 4. That score supports testing with reasonable empiric therapy while results are pending.

checks.q: A 19-year-old with mononucleosis was given amoxicillin elsewhere and now has a diffuse itchy rash. What is the explanation?
choices: A true IgE penicillin allergy requiring epinephrine
A characteristic non-allergic rash seen when aminopenicillins are given in EBV infection
checks.why: Aminopenicillins produce a widespread maculopapular rash in a substantial share of EBV patients, roughly a third to half in modern studies. It is not a true allergy and does not carry anaphylaxis risk, and it lacks the mucosal blistering of Stevens-Johnson.

checks.q: An adult arrives sitting forward on his hands, drooling, with a muffled voice, fever, and rapidly worsening throat pain over 6 hours. What should be avoided?
choices: Depressing the tongue for a thorough oral exam
Summoning personnel able to secure an airway
checks.why: This is epiglottitis. Instrumenting the oropharynx can trigger laryngospasm and complete obstruction. Upright positioning, oxygen and airway-capable help are all correct.

lessons.title: Mouth and teeth: pain, pus and knocked-out teeth
lessons.body:
## How a tooth hurts

A tooth is enamel over dentin over a living core of nerve and vessel (the **pulp**). Bacteria erode enamel into a cavity (**caries**). Once decay reaches the pulp, the nerve inflames — **pulpitis**.

**Reversible pulpitis** hurts briefly with cold or sweets and stops within seconds. **Irreversible pulpitis** aches for minutes after the stimulus, often spontaneously, and is worse lying down because blood flow to the head increases. That positional clue is a useful history question.

When the pulp dies the infection pushes out the root tip into bone, producing a **periapical abscess**: constant throbbing, a tooth that hurts to tap or bite on, swelling of the gum, and sometimes fever. Drainage is the definitive treatment; antibiotics such as amoxicillin or clindamycin are added when there is facial swelling, fever or spread.

> **Trap:** Dental infection that spreads produces swelling below the jaw, an elevated tongue, trouble swallowing or drooling. That is Ludwig angina territory, and the concern shifts from the tooth to the airway.

## Avulsed and fractured teeth

A knocked-out **permanent** tooth is a true time emergency. The ligament cells on the root surface die quickly, and survival falls sharply after `30-60 minutes` out of the socket. Reimplantation within `6 hours` is the outer limit, with best results under `1 hour`.

Handle by the **crown only**, never the root. If dirty, rinse gently for `10 seconds` in saline or milk — never scrub. Reimplant into the socket immediately if possible. If not, transport in cold milk, Hank's balanced salt solution, or saline; water is the worst choice because it bursts the cells. Then urgent dental follow-up and a tetanus check.

**Primary (baby) teeth are never reimplanted** — doing so can damage the permanent tooth bud underneath.

Fractures are graded by depth: enamel only (cosmetic), into dentin (sensitive, yellow layer visible), and into the pulp with a pink or bleeding spot in the center, which needs same-day dental care.

## Alveolar osteitis

**Dry socket** shows up `2-5 days` after an extraction, most often a lower molar. The protective clot dissolves and exposes bone. Severe throbbing pain radiating to the ear, bad taste, and an empty-looking socket. Smoking and straw use raise risk. Treatment is irrigation and a medicated dressing, which relieves pain within minutes, plus dental follow-up.

## Oral lesions worth recognizing

- **Aphthous ulcers (canker sores)**: shallow, round, gray-white center with a red halo, on soft non-keratinized mucosa, painful, heal in `7-14 days`, not contagious.
- **Herpes labialis (cold sore)**: vesicles on the lip border or hard palate, recurrent, triggered by sun or stress, contagious.
- **Oral candidiasis (thrush)**: creamy white plaques that **scrape off** leaving a red raw base. Think inhaled steroids, antibiotics, diabetes, dentures, or immunosuppression. Treat with nystatin swish or fluconazole.
- **Leukoplakia**: a white patch that **cannot be scraped off**. Tobacco-associated and potentially precancerous, so it is biopsied.
- **Erythroplakia**: a red velvety patch, less common but with an even higher chance of dysplasia.

> **Key:** Scrapes off equals thrush. Will not scrape off equals leukoplakia and a biopsy referral.

## TMJ disorder

Pain in front of the ear, clicking or locking with opening, jaw muscle tenderness, headache, worse with chewing and often with night clenching. Normal opening is about `40-50 mm`. Treat with soft diet, heat, NSAIDs, stopping gum and wide yawning, and a night guard. Sudden inability to close after a wide yawn is a dislocation that needs reduction.
keyPoints: Pain lingering minutes after cold and worse lying down is irreversible pulpitis; a tooth painful to tap suggests periapical abscess.
Avulsed permanent tooth: handle the crown, rinse 10 seconds, reimplant within 1 hour and no later than 6 hours; transport in milk, not water.
Primary teeth are never reimplanted because of damage to the permanent tooth bud.
Dry socket appears 2-5 days after extraction with severe pain radiating to the ear; irrigation and a medicated dressing relieve it quickly.
White plaque that scrapes off is thrush; a white patch that does not scrape off is leukoplakia and needs biopsy.

checks.q: A 12-year-old has a permanent central incisor knocked out on a field 20 minutes ago. What is the best immediate action?
choices: Scrub the root clean with a toothbrush and tap water
Discard the tooth and refer for an implant later
Hold the tooth by the crown, rinse briefly, and reimplant it into the socket
Store the tooth dry in gauze for the dental visit
checks.why: Periodontal ligament cells survive best when the tooth returns to the socket within the hour. Scrubbing destroys those cells, tap water bursts them, and dry storage kills them fastest.

checks.q: A patient on inhaled corticosteroids has creamy white plaques on the tongue that wipe off, leaving a raw red surface. What is this?
checks.why: Plaques that scrape off to reveal a red base are thrush, common with inhaled steroids. Leukoplakia and erythroplakia do not scrape off, and aphthous ulcers are craters, not plaques.

checks.q: Three days after a lower molar extraction, a smoker returns with severe throbbing pain radiating to the ear and an empty-looking socket. What is the diagnosis?
checks.why: Loss of the clot 2-5 days after extraction exposes bone, causing dry socket. Ludwig angina involves floor-of-mouth swelling and airway risk, and pulpitis requires a tooth still present.

lessons.title: Neck lumps, hoarse voices and blocked airways
lessons.body:
## Reading a neck mass by age and time

Three questions carry most of the weight: how old is the patient, how long has it been there, and where exactly is it?

In children, most neck masses are **reactive lymph nodes** from an infection, or congenital. In adults over `40`, a firm neck mass present for more than `2-3 weeks` without an obvious infection is assumed to be cancer until proven otherwise.

Reassuring node features: small (under `1 cm`), soft, mobile, tender, appearing with an illness and shrinking within `2-4 weeks`. Worrying features: larger than `1.5-2 cm`, firm or hard, fixed to underlying tissue, painless, growing, present over `4-6 weeks`, or in the supraclavicular area — a supraclavicular node in an adult is a chest or abdominal cancer until disproven.

> **Trap:** The first move for a suspicious adult neck mass is **not** an excisional biopsy. Cutting into a nodal metastasis can seed the field. The path is exam of the throat and nasopharynx, imaging, and fine-needle aspiration.

## Congenital masses

- **Thyroglossal duct cyst**: midline, near the hyoid, **moves upward when the patient swallows or sticks out the tongue** because it is tethered to the tongue base.
- **Branchial cleft cyst**: lateral, along the front border of the sternocleidomastoid, often noticed when it swells during an upper respiratory infection.
- **Cystic hygroma (lymphatic malformation)**: soft, compressible, transilluminates, usually in the posterior triangle of an infant.

## Thyroid and salivary glands

A **thyroid nodule** moves with swallowing and sits low and midline or just off it. Most are benign. Evaluation is a TSH first, then ultrasound; a low TSH suggests a hot functioning nodule and prompts a scan, while normal or high TSH with suspicious ultrasound features leads to fine-needle aspiration. Higher risk comes with age under `20` or over `70`, male sex, a hard fixed nodule, hoarseness, and prior neck radiation.

**Sialadenitis** is infection of a salivary gland, most often the parotid, in a dehydrated older or postoperative patient. The gland is swollen, hot and tender, and pus can be milked from the duct. Treatment is hydration, warm compresses, massage, sour candy to stimulate flow, and antibiotics covering `Staph aureus`.

**Sialolithiasis** is a duct stone, most often in the submandibular gland because its secretions are thick and it drains uphill. The giveaway is swelling and pain that flare **with meals** and settle afterward.

## Head and neck cancer risk

Tobacco and alcohol multiply each other's risk. HPV type 16 now drives a large share of tonsil and tongue-base cancers, often in younger nonsmokers. Other factors are betel nut, prior radiation, and chronic sun exposure for lip cancer.

Red flags that push toward urgent ENT referral: a neck mass over `2 weeks` in an adult, hoarseness beyond `2-3 weeks`, an ulcer that will not heal, painful or difficult swallowing, unexplained ear pain with a normal ear exam (**referred otalgia**), and unexplained weight loss.

> **Key:** Hoarseness lasting more than 2-3 weeks in an adult who smokes earns laryngoscopy, not another round of reflux medication.

## Foreign bodies and obstruction

Swallowed coins are the classic pediatric object and usually pass, but a **button battery** in the esophagus burns tissue within `2 hours` and is removed emergently. Sharp objects and anything lodged at the cricopharyngeus also come out.

For airway obstruction, the dividing line is air movement. A patient who can cough forcefully, speak, or cry is moving air — encourage coughing and do not intervene. Silence, a weak cough, or the universal choking sign means abdominal thrusts in an adult or child over `1`, and back blows with chest thrusts in an infant. When the patient goes unresponsive, begin CPR and look in the mouth each time before ventilating, removing only an object you can see.
keyPoints: An adult neck mass firm and present over 2-3 weeks is cancer until proven otherwise; supraclavicular nodes are especially ominous.
Avoid excisional biopsy first; evaluate with exam, imaging and fine-needle aspiration.
A midline mass that rises when the tongue protrudes is a thyroglossal duct cyst; a lateral mass along the sternocleidomastoid is a branchial cleft cyst.
Salivary swelling and pain that spike with meals suggest a duct stone, most often submandibular.
A button battery in the esophagus causes burns within 2 hours and is an emergent removal.

checks.q: A 62-year-old smoker has a firm, painless, fixed 3 cm lateral neck mass present for 6 weeks. What is the most appropriate next step?
choices: A 10-day course of amoxicillin-clavulanate and reassessment
Excisional biopsy of the mass in clinic
Upper aerodigestive exam with imaging and fine-needle aspiration
checks.why: Age, smoking, firmness, fixation and duration all point to malignancy. Excisional biopsy first can seed tumor and compromise definitive surgery, and antibiotics delay diagnosis.

checks.q: A 3-year-old swallowed a button battery that is lodged in the esophagus. Why is this urgent?
choices: It causes caustic tissue injury within about 2 hours
It will dissolve and release toxic mercury vapor
It usually blocks the airway completely
It cannot be seen on plain radiographs
checks.why: Current flowing through mucosa generates hydroxide and burns tissue within roughly 2 hours, risking perforation. Batteries are radiopaque with a halo sign, and esophageal lodging does not itself obstruct the airway.

cards.front: What is the eye's vital sign, and how is it recorded?
cards.back: Visual acuity, measured and documented for each eye separately with corrective lenses on, before any other part of the eye exam.

cards.front: What is the normal range for intraocular pressure?
cards.back: 10-21 mmHg. Above 21 is abnormal; above 40 with pain suggests acute angle-closure glaucoma.

cards.front: During the swinging flashlight test, one pupil dilates when the light reaches it. What is this called and what does it localize?
cards.back: A relative afferent pupillary defect, or Marcus Gunn pupil. It localizes disease to the retina or optic nerve of that eye.

cards.front: What does 20/40 vision mean?
cards.back: The patient sees at 20 feet what an eye with normal acuity sees at 40 feet.

cards.front: Blurred vision improves when the patient looks through a pinhole. What does that tell you?
cards.back: The problem is refractive or in the clear media, not in the retina or optic nerve.

cards.front: Which three parts of the eye exam are skipped when globe rupture is suspected?
cards.back: Tonometry, lid retraction or forceful opening, and further drops or dye. Pressure on the eye can extrude its contents.

cards.front: Why is proparacaine never prescribed for home use?
cards.back: Topical anesthetics delay corneal epithelial healing and mask a worsening injury. They are for the exam only.

cards.front: What discharge pattern separates bacterial from viral conjunctivitis?
cards.back: Bacterial gives thick yellow-green discharge with lids stuck shut on waking. Viral gives watery discharge with a tender node in front of the ear.

cards.front: Which symptom is the strongest clue for allergic conjunctivitis?
cards.back: Itching, with stringy clear discharge in both eyes and a seasonal pattern.

cards.front: What does ciliary flush look like and what does it mean?
cards.back: Redness concentrated in a ring around the cornea. It signals intraocular inflammation such as uveitis, keratitis or angle-closure glaucoma, not simple conjunctivitis.

cards.front: Name the five classic features of acute angle-closure glaucoma.
cards.back: Severe pain, nausea and vomiting, halos around lights, a hazy cornea, and a mid-dilated poorly reactive pupil. IOP is often 40-70 mmHg.

cards.front: Fluorescein shows a branching dendritic pattern. What is it and what is contraindicated?
cards.back: Herpes simplex keratitis. Topical corticosteroids are contraindicated because they can drive the ulcer to perforation.

cards.front: How do you distinguish scleritis from episcleritis at the bedside?
cards.back: Scleritis has deep boring pain that wakes the patient, a violet hue, and does not blanch with phenylephrine. Episcleritis is mild and blanches.

cards.front: A contact lens wearer has a red painful eye. What is assumed and what must not be done?
cards.back: Assume a corneal ulcer, often Pseudomonas. Remove the lens, cover Pseudomonas, and never patch the eye.

cards.front: Which conjunctivitis presents with copious thick pus 12-24 hours after exposure?
cards.back: Gonococcal conjunctivitis. It can perforate the cornea within a day and requires systemic therapy, not drops alone.

cards.front: Which three symptoms in order describe a retinal detachment?
cards.back: A sudden shower of floaters, flashes of light, then a painless dark curtain moving across the visual field.

cards.front: What fundus finding defines central retinal artery occlusion?
cards.back: A pale retina with a cherry-red spot at the macula, plus an RAPD and painless profound vision loss.

cards.front: How long before retinal damage becomes irreversible in CRAO?
cards.back: Around 90 minutes. CRAO is treated with stroke-level urgency.

cards.front: What does a blood-and-thunder fundus indicate?
cards.back: Central retinal vein occlusion: hemorrhages in all four quadrants with a swollen optic disc, on a background of hypertension, diabetes or glaucoma.

cards.front: Which symptoms suggest giant cell arteritis, and in what age group?
cards.back: Age over 50, usually over 70: temporal headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, polymyalgia stiffness, elevated ESR and CRP.

cards.front: When are steroids started in suspected giant cell arteritis?
cards.back: Immediately, before the temporal artery biopsy. The biopsy remains informative for days afterward, and the other eye can be lost within days.

cards.front: How does optic neuritis typically present?
cards.back: A woman aged 20-40 with vision dimming over hours to days, washed-out color vision, pain with eye movement, and an RAPD. About half develop multiple sclerosis.

cards.front: How long does amaurosis fugax last and what does it predict?
cards.back: 2-30 minutes of painless monocular loss with full recovery. It is a TIA of the eye, usually carotid, and predicts stroke.

cards.front: What is the pH target after irrigating a chemical eye burn?
cards.back: pH 7.0-7.4, checked about 5 minutes after irrigation stops. If it is off, keep irrigating.

cards.front: How much fluid and how long for chemical eye irrigation, and which agent is worse?
cards.back: At least 1-2 liters per eye over 15-30 minutes. Alkali is worse than acid because it keeps penetrating rather than self-limiting.

cards.front: Vertical linear corneal scratches are seen on fluorescein. What must you do?
cards.back: Evert the upper lid and remove the retained foreign body scraping the cornea with each blink.

cards.front: Which histories should make you suspect an intraocular foreign body?
cards.back: High-speed grinding, hammering metal on metal, or weed trimming. Order CT, never MRI, even if the eye looks and feels normal.

cards.front: How is a hyphema managed, and when is rebleeding most likely?
cards.back: Head elevated 30-45 degrees, rigid shield, avoid aspirin and NSAIDs, monitor IOP. Rebleeding peaks on days 3-5.

cards.front: Which findings suggest an orbital blowout fracture?
cards.back: Pain and restriction on upward gaze, diplopia, numbness of the cheek and upper lip from infraorbital nerve injury, and sometimes a sunken eye.

cards.front: Why is a child with a blowout fracture, vomiting and bradycardia a surgical emergency?
cards.back: Springy bone traps the inferior rectus tightly and stimulates the vagus. Muscle release is needed within 24-48 hours to prevent necrosis.

cards.front: Name four signs of globe rupture.
cards.back: Teardrop or irregular pupil, a soft eye, dark uveal tissue at the wound, and a positive Seidel sign with fluorescein diluted by leaking aqueous.

cards.front: Why does the eustachian tube make young children prone to otitis media?
cards.back: In children it is short, floppy and nearly horizontal, so nasal secretions reach the middle ear easily and drain poorly. It angles downward by adolescence.

cards.front: Which bedside maneuver points to otitis externa rather than otitis media?
cards.back: Pain on pulling the pinna or pressing the tragus. That tenderness localizes inflammation to the canal skin.

cards.front: What is the first-line antibiotic and dose for acute otitis media in a child?
cards.back: High-dose amoxicillin 80-90 mg/kg/day divided twice daily; amoxicillin-clavulanate if the child had antibiotics within the last 30 days.

cards.front: What finding is required to call a drum acutely infected rather than just red?
cards.back: A bulging tympanic membrane with loss of landmarks and reduced mobility on pneumatic otoscopy, plus acute illness signs.

cards.front: A diabetic has severe ear pain, drainage and granulation tissue in the canal. What is this?
cards.back: Malignant or necrotizing otitis externa, infection spreading to skull base bone. It requires imaging and IV antibiotics, not drops.

cards.front: When is ear irrigation for cerumen contraindicated?
cards.back: When the tympanic membrane may be perforated or when tympanostomy tubes are in place.

cards.front: Which ear findings suggest mastoiditis?
cards.back: The pinna pushed outward and forward, with redness, swelling and tenderness over the mastoid behind the ear. It needs CT, IV antibiotics and ENT.

cards.front: What is a cholesteatoma and how does it present?
cards.back: A growing ball of trapped skin cells in the middle ear. Painless, chronically draining, foul-smelling ear with progressive hearing loss. It erodes bone and is treated surgically.

cards.front: Which way does the Weber test lateralize in conductive versus sensorineural loss?
cards.back: Toward the affected ear in conductive loss; away from the affected ear in sensorineural loss. Use a 512 Hz fork on the forehead.

cards.front: What does a reversed Rinne mean?
cards.back: Bone conduction lasts longer than air conduction in that ear, which indicates conductive hearing loss.

cards.front: Why is sudden sensorineural hearing loss an emergency?
cards.back: Loss developing over 72 hours or less has a narrow treatment window. High-dose oral steroids started within days, and no later than 2 weeks, offer the only real chance of recovery.

cards.front: How long does a BPPV episode last and what triggers it?
cards.back: 10-60 seconds, triggered by head position changes such as rolling over or tipping the head back. Hearing stays normal.

cards.front: Which maneuver diagnoses BPPV and which treats it?
cards.back: Dix-Hallpike diagnoses it by reproducing delayed fatigable rotary nystagmus. The Epley maneuver repositions the crystals and treats it.

cards.front: What is the Meniere triad and how long do attacks last?
cards.back: Episodic vertigo, fluctuating low-frequency hearing loss, and ear fullness with roaring tinnitus. Attacks last 20 minutes to 12 hours.

cards.front: How does vestibular neuritis differ from BPPV?
cards.back: Vestibular neuritis causes constant severe vertigo lasting days after a viral illness, with normal hearing. BPPV is brief and positional.

cards.front: Which three HINTS findings point to a central cause of vertigo?
cards.back: A normal head-impulse test, direction-changing nystagmus, and skew deviation on cover-uncover. Inability to walk unassisted is also central until proven otherwise.

cards.front: Where do most nosebleeds originate and what fraction are they?
cards.back: Kiesselbach plexus on the anterior nasal septum, accounting for about 90% of epistaxis.

cards.front: Exactly where and how long should a patient pinch for a nosebleed?
cards.back: On the soft cartilage below the bony bridge, leaning forward, for 10-15 uninterrupted minutes by the clock.

cards.front: Why is silver nitrate cautery applied to only one side of the septum?
cards.back: Cauterizing both sides at the same site can destroy the septal blood supply and cause perforation.

cards.front: What suggests a posterior nosebleed?
cards.back: Heavy or bilateral bleeding that keeps running down the throat despite a well-placed anterior pack, usually in older, hypertensive or anticoagulated patients.

cards.front: What are the three criteria that suggest bacterial rather than viral sinusitis?
cards.back: Symptoms 10 days or more without improvement; severe onset with fever 39 C plus purulent discharge for 3-4 days; or double worsening after initial improvement.

cards.front: What is the most effective single medication for allergic rhinitis?
cards.back: An intranasal corticosteroid. Second-generation antihistamines add relief for sneezing and itch.

cards.front: What causes rhinitis medicamentosa and how is it fixed?
cards.back: Rebound congestion from using a topical decongestant spray longer than 3 days. Treatment is stopping the spray.

cards.front: Which findings mean sinusitis has spread to the orbit?
cards.back: Eyelid swelling with pain on eye movement, proptosis, or double vision. That is orbital cellulitis, needing CT and IV antibiotics.

cards.front: List the four Centor criteria.
cards.back: Fever, absence of cough, tonsillar exudate or swelling, and tender anterior cervical lymph nodes. One point each.

cards.front: How does the McIsaac modification adjust the Centor score?
cards.back: Add 1 point for age 3-14, add 0 for age 15-44, and subtract 1 for age 45 and older.

cards.front: What is first-line treatment and duration for confirmed group A strep pharyngitis?
cards.back: Penicillin V or amoxicillin for 10 days. Use a first-generation cephalosporin or azithromycin for penicillin allergy.

cards.front: Which mononucleosis features change management?
cards.back: Splenomegaly in about half means no contact sports for 3-4 weeks, and aminopenicillins produce a widespread non-allergic rash.

cards.front: Which way does the uvula deviate in peritonsillar abscess, and what else is present?
cards.back: Away from the swollen side. Also one-sided pain, a hot-potato muffled voice, trismus and drooling. Treatment is drainage plus antibiotics.

cards.front: Who gets retropharyngeal abscess and how does it look?
cards.back: Children under 6 after pharyngitis or an oral puncture. Fever, neck stiffness, refusal to move the neck, painful swallowing, and widened prevertebral soft tissue on lateral neck film.

cards.front: What are the three Ds of epiglottitis and the posture that goes with them?
cards.back: Drooling, dysphagia and distress, with the patient upright in the tripod position leaning on the hands. Stridor is a late sign.

cards.front: What is Ludwig angina and what drives management?
cards.back: Rapidly spreading infection of the floor of the mouth, usually from a lower molar, elevating the tongue. Airway comes first, then IV antibiotics and drainage.

cards.front: How do reversible and irreversible pulpitis differ?
cards.back: Reversible pain stops within seconds of removing the stimulus. Irreversible pain lingers for minutes, occurs spontaneously, and is worse lying down.

cards.front: What is the time window for reimplanting an avulsed permanent tooth?
cards.back: Best within 1 hour, with survival dropping sharply after 30-60 minutes out of the socket and roughly 6 hours as the outer limit.

cards.front: How should an avulsed tooth be handled and transported?
cards.back: Hold the crown only, rinse gently for 10 seconds, reimplant if possible, otherwise transport in cold milk, Hank's solution or saline. Never water, never scrub.

cards.front: When is dry socket expected and how does it feel?
cards.back: 2-5 days after an extraction, usually a lower molar. Severe throbbing pain radiating to the ear with a bad taste and an empty-looking socket.

cards.front: A white oral patch will not scrape off. What is it and what is the next step?
cards.back: Leukoplakia, tobacco-associated and potentially precancerous. It needs biopsy. Thrush, by contrast, scrapes off leaving a red base.

cards.front: How does temporomandibular joint disorder present, and what is normal mouth opening?
cards.back: Pain in front of the ear, clicking or locking, jaw muscle tenderness and headache worse with chewing. Normal opening is about 40-50 mm.

cards.front: Which neck mass features in an adult are worrying?
cards.back: Larger than 1.5-2 cm, firm or hard, fixed, painless, growing, present over 4-6 weeks, or supraclavicular. Assume cancer after 2-3 weeks without an infection.

cards.front: Why is excisional biopsy avoided as the first step for a suspicious adult neck mass?
cards.back: Cutting into a nodal metastasis can seed the surgical field and compromise definitive treatment. Use exam, imaging and fine-needle aspiration instead.

cards.front: A midline neck mass rises when the patient sticks out the tongue. What is it?
cards.back: A thyroglossal duct cyst, tethered to the tongue base near the hyoid bone.

quiz.q: What is the normal range of intraocular pressure in an adult eye?
quiz.why: Normal IOP is 10-21 mmHg. 22-35 is elevated, 40-70 is the range seen in acute angle-closure crisis, and single-digit pressure suggests a leaking or ruptured globe.

quiz.q: A patient complains of blurred vision. Looking through a pinhole card sharpens the image considerably. What does this finding suggest?
quiz.why: The pinhole narrows the light beam and bypasses refractive error and media irregularity, so improvement points there. Retinal and optic nerve disease does not improve with a pinhole.

quiz.q: Which of the following can produce a relative afferent pupillary defect?
quiz.why: An RAPD requires reduced signal transmission along the retina or optic nerve, which optic neuritis causes. Cataracts, corneal scars and refractive error block or blur light but leave the afferent signal intact.

quiz.q: A patient struck in the eye has an irregular, teardrop-shaped pupil and a very soft globe. Which step would be most harmful?
choices: Measuring intraocular pressure with a tonometer
quiz.why: Applanation on a ruptured globe can extrude intraocular contents. A rigid shield, antiemetics to prevent straining, and IV antibiotics are all standard for suspected rupture.

quiz.q: Which type of conjunctivitis is most strongly suggested by intense itching and stringy clear discharge in both eyes?
quiz.why: Itching is the hallmark of allergic conjunctivitis. Bacterial discharge is thick and purulent, gonococcal is hyperacute and copious, and herpetic keratitis causes pain rather than itch.

quiz.q: A 24-year-old with low back stiffness has a painful red eye with ciliary flush, a small sluggish pupil, and photophobia so severe that shining light in the other eye hurts. What is the most likely diagnosis?
quiz.why: Consensual photophobia, ciliary flush and a small sluggish pupil define anterior uveitis, which associates with ankylosing spondylitis. Conjunctivitis lacks ciliary flush and episcleritis is not painful.

quiz.q: A contact lens wearer presents with a painful red eye and a corneal infiltrate. Which management step is incorrect?
quiz.why: Patching creates a warm moist chamber that accelerates Pseudomonas growth and is contraindicated in lens-related ulcers. Lens removal, Pseudomonas coverage and urgent follow-up are all correct.

quiz.q: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis reports deep boring eye pain that wakes her at night. The redness has a violet hue and does not blanch with phenylephrine. What does this indicate?
quiz.why: Non-blanching violet redness with night-waking boring pain in a patient with rheumatoid arthritis is scleritis. Episcleritis blanches and is mild, and a subconjunctival hemorrhage is painless and bright red.

quiz.q: Which symptom sequence is characteristic of retinal detachment?
choices: Floaters and flashes followed by a painless curtain over part of the field
Severe pain with halos around lights
Burning and itching in both eyes
quiz.why: Vitreous traction produces photopsia and floaters before the retina separates, creating a field defect described as a curtain. Halos with pain describe angle closure, and itching describes allergy.

quiz.q: A 68-year-old with hypertension and diabetes has moderate painless vision loss over several hours. The fundus shows hemorrhages in all four quadrants with a swollen disc. What is the diagnosis?
quiz.why: The blood-and-thunder fundus with diffuse hemorrhage and disc edema is CRVO. CRAO produces a pale retina with a cherry-red spot, and optic neuritis causes pain with eye movement in a younger patient.

quiz.q: A 74-year-old reports jaw pain while chewing, scalp tenderness, and transient blurring in one eye. ESR is 88. What is the priority action?
choices: Schedule outpatient ophthalmology in two weeks
quiz.why: This is giant cell arteritis, which can blind the fellow eye within days. Systemic steroids start immediately and biopsy follows. Topical drops do nothing for arteritis, and delay risks permanent loss.

quiz.q: A 32-year-old woman has vision that dimmed over two days, faded red color perception, aching with eye movement, and an RAPD. Which additional study is most appropriate?
choices: MRI of the brain and orbits
quiz.why: This is optic neuritis, and roughly half of these patients develop multiple sclerosis, so MRI looks for demyelinating lesions. Carotid studies fit amaurosis fugax, and gonioscopy fits angle closure.

quiz.q: After irrigating an alkali eye burn, what pH range confirms adequate irrigation?
quiz.why: The target tear film pH is 7.0-7.4, rechecked about 5 minutes after stopping. Acidic or alkaline readings mean chemical remains and irrigation continues.

quiz.q: A machinist was grinding metal without eye protection. His eye is comfortable and acuity is 20/20, but he felt something hit it. What is the most appropriate next step?
choices: Obtain an MRI of the orbits
Obtain a CT of the orbits
quiz.why: High-speed metal can penetrate with minimal symptoms, so CT is used to look for an intraocular foreign body. MRI is contraindicated because a ferromagnetic fragment can move, and patching delays diagnosis.

quiz.q: A patient with a traumatic hyphema asks how to position himself at home. What is the correct instruction?
choices: Lie completely flat to reduce pressure
quiz.why: Elevating the head lets blood settle inferiorly and out of the visual axis, and reduces pressure spikes. Lying flat or head-down disperses blood across the pupil and worsens vision.

quiz.q: A 10-year-old struck by a softball cannot look upward, is vomiting, and has a heart rate of 46. What best explains the vomiting and bradycardia?
choices: Vagal stimulation from an entrapped extraocular muscle
quiz.why: Trapdoor orbital fractures in children pinch the inferior rectus, triggering the oculocardiac reflex with nausea, vomiting and bradycardia. It demands surgical release within 24-48 hours.

quiz.q: Which organism most commonly causes otitis externa?
quiz.why: Pseudomonas, along with Staph aureus, dominates canal infections after water exposure. Strep pneumoniae is a middle-ear pathogen, and EBV and Candida cause pharyngeal and oral disease.

quiz.q: A 3-year-old with a cold now has fever and ear pain. The drum is bulging with poor mobility. He has had no antibiotics in the past year. What is first-line therapy?
choices: High-dose amoxicillin 80-90 mg/kg/day divided twice daily
quiz.why: High-dose amoxicillin covers Strep pneumoniae including intermediate-resistance strains and is first-line for acute otitis media. Drops do not reach the middle ear through an intact drum, and IV therapy is for complications.

quiz.q: A 70-year-old diabetic has weeks of severe ear pain, foul drainage, and granulation tissue at the bone-cartilage junction of the canal. What is the concern?
choices: Necrotizing otitis externa involving skull base bone
quiz.why: Pain out of proportion with granulation tissue in a diabetic signals osteomyelitis of the skull base, requiring imaging and prolonged IV antibiotics. Topical therapy alone is inadequate.

quiz.q: A child with a long history of ear drainage now has a painless, foul-smelling discharge and worsening hearing. The drum shows a retraction pocket filled with white debris. What is this?
quiz.why: Trapped keratin in a retraction pocket forms a cholesteatoma, which erodes bone and is surgical. Acute otitis media is painful and acute, and effusion causes no foul drainage.

quiz.q: Which tuning fork frequency is standard for Weber and Rinne testing?
quiz.why: The 512 Hz fork balances audible tone with adequate duration. The 128 Hz fork is used for vibration sense in neurologic exams, and higher frequencies decay too quickly.

quiz.q: A patient's Weber lateralizes to the right and Rinne shows air conduction greater than bone conduction bilaterally. What is the interpretation?
quiz.why: A normal Rinne in both ears rules out conductive loss, so lateralization away from the left means left sensorineural loss. Right conductive loss would reverse the Rinne on the right.

quiz.q: A 40-year-old awakens with muffled hearing in one ear that developed over a few hours, with no pain and a normal drum. Audiometry confirms sensorineural loss. What is the appropriate action?
choices: Prescribe a decongestant and recheck in a month
Irrigate the canal for possible wax
quiz.why: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss has a narrow treatment window; steroids are most effective started within days and lose benefit after about 2 weeks. Waiting or treating for wax squanders that window.

quiz.q: A 55-year-old has continuous vertigo and nystagmus. His head-impulse test is normal, nystagmus changes direction with gaze, and he cannot stand without falling. What is the best interpretation?
choices: A central cause such as cerebellar stroke
quiz.why: A normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus and truncal instability are each central signs. BPPV lasts under a minute and is positional, and neuritis produces an abnormal head impulse with unidirectional nystagmus.

quiz.q: Where should a patient compress the nose to stop a typical nosebleed?
choices: On the soft cartilage just below the bony bridge
On the bony bridge between the eyes
At the base of the nostrils against the upper lip
On the forehead above the eyebrows
quiz.why: Kiesselbach plexus lies on the anterior septum behind the soft cartilage, so pinching there tamponades it. Squeezing the bony bridge applies no pressure to the bleeding site.

quiz.q: An 80-year-old on warfarin has bleeding from both nostrils and blood streaming down his throat despite a well-placed anterior pack. What is the next step?
choices: Reapply direct pressure for another 20 minutes
Discharge with saline gel and follow-up
Place a posterior balloon, admit and involve ENT
Apply silver nitrate to both sides of the septum
quiz.why: Failure of an adequate anterior pack with posterior drainage identifies a sphenopalatine source needing posterior packing and monitored admission. Bilateral cautery risks septal perforation, and discharge risks significant blood loss.

quiz.q: A patient has had nasal congestion, purulent discharge and facial pressure for 4 days without fever. What is the most appropriate management?
choices: Symptomatic care with saline irrigation and analgesia
quiz.why: Four days of moderate symptoms without fever is consistent with viral sinusitis, which resolves by day 7-10. Antibiotics are reserved for 10+ days without improvement, severe onset with fever 39 C, or double worsening.

quiz.q: A patient with a week of sinusitis now has eyelid swelling, pain with eye movement, and mild proptosis. What is the most appropriate action?
choices: Add an oral antihistamine and warm compresses
Continue oral antibiotics and recheck in 3 days
Obtain CT of the orbits and sinuses and start IV antibiotics
quiz.why: Pain on eye movement and proptosis mark orbital cellulitis behind the septum, which threatens vision and can extend intracranially. Topical and oral outpatient therapy is inadequate for post-septal infection.

quiz.q: Which finding argues most strongly against group A streptococcal pharyngitis?
quiz.why: Absence of cough is a Centor criterion, so a prominent cough shifts the picture toward a viral cause. Exudate, tender anterior nodes and fever all support strep.

quiz.q: A 9-year-old has fever, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior nodes and no cough. What is the McIsaac score?
quiz.why: All four Centor criteria give 4 points, and age 3-14 adds 1 more for a total of 5. That score supports rapid testing, with culture backup in children if the rapid test is negative.

quiz.q: A 17-year-old has severe right-sided throat pain, a muffled voice, difficulty opening his mouth, and a uvula deviated to the left. What is the diagnosis and treatment?
quiz.why: Unilateral swelling pushing the uvula to the opposite side with trismus and a hot-potato voice is a peritonsillar abscess, treated by needle aspiration or incision plus antibiotics. Retropharyngeal abscess affects young children and does not deviate the uvula this way.
