quiz.q: An unvaccinated 5-year-old has 6 hours of fever, drooling, and distress, and sits leaning forward on his hands refusing to lie down. What should be done first?
choices: Lay him supine and examine the pharynx with a tongue blade
Obtain blood cultures and start IV fluids in triage
Send him unaccompanied to radiology for a lateral neck film
Keep him upright and calm while assembling airway-capable personnel
quiz.why: Epiglottitis can obstruct completely if the child is agitated or the airway instrumented. Position of comfort with airway expertise present comes first; procedures and imaging follow only in a controlled setting.

quiz.q: Which storage medium is best for an avulsed permanent tooth that cannot be immediately reimplanted?
quiz.why: Milk approximates physiologic osmolality and preserves periodontal ligament cells, as does Hank's solution or saline. Water lyses the cells, dry storage kills them fastest, and peroxide is cytotoxic.

quiz.q: A 5-year-old knocks out a primary incisor. What is the correct management?
choices: Reimplant it immediately into the socket
Do not reimplant it; arrange dental follow-up
Splint it back after soaking in peroxide
Reimplant only if it has been out less than 30 minutes
quiz.why: Reimplanting a primary tooth risks damaging the developing permanent tooth bud beneath it, so baby teeth are never replaced. The 1-hour and 6-hour windows apply only to permanent teeth.

quiz.q: A patient with a dental infection now has a firm swelling under the jaw, an elevated tongue, drooling and difficulty swallowing. What is the priority?
choices: Airway assessment and preparation for a difficult airway
Incision and drainage of the involved tooth in clinic
quiz.why: This is Ludwig angina, where floor-of-mouth swelling displaces the tongue and can obstruct the airway. Airway control precedes IV antibiotics and drainage; outpatient management is unsafe.

quiz.q: A firm, painless, fixed neck mass has been present for 8 weeks in a 60-year-old smoker. What is the most appropriate first step?
choices: Upper aerodigestive tract examination with imaging and fine-needle aspiration
quiz.why: Duration, fixation and smoking history point to metastatic carcinoma. Open biopsy first can seed the field, antibiotics delay diagnosis, and observation wastes time in a treatable cancer.

quiz.q: A patient reports swelling and pain in the area under the jaw that flares during meals and subsides afterward. What is the most likely cause?
quiz.why: Meal-triggered swelling and pain reflect obstructed salivary outflow, most often a submandibular stone because those secretions are thick and drain uphill. Bacterial parotitis causes constant swelling with expressible pus, and a thyroglossal cyst is midline and moves with tongue protrusion.

scenarios.title: Triage: 54-year-old with a painful red eye and vomiting
scenarios.intro: It is 9 p.m. A 54-year-old woman walks into triage holding a hand over her right eye. She says the pain started about two hours ago while she was watching a movie in a dark theater, and she has vomited twice on the way in. She is not a contact lens wearer and has no eye history beyond reading glasses.

steps.prompt: She is grimacing, tearing, and says the overhead lights make it worse. Her right eye looks red and the cornea has a steamy, hazy appearance. What do you do first?

choices.text: Measure visual acuity in each eye and check the pupils
choices.feedback: Correct. Acuity is the eye's vital sign, and it takes under a minute. Pupil findings here will matter enormously.

choices.text: Place her in a room and give an antiemetic before any eye exam
choices.feedback: Comfort matters, but vomiting is a clue here, not just a symptom. Do not let it delay the two-minute exam that names the diagnosis.

choices.text: Instill fluorescein and look for a corneal abrasion
choices.feedback: Premature. Her story points inward, not to the surface, and staining before acuity and pupil check skips the information that sorts this.

choices.text: Reassure her this is likely a migraine and place her in the waiting room
choices.feedback: Harmful. Headache with vomiting and a red, hazy eye is not a migraine until an eye emergency is excluded.

steps.prompt: Acuity is 20/30 on the left and counting fingers on the right. The right pupil is mid-dilated at about 5 mm and barely reacts. The left pupil is 3 mm and brisk. She says lights have rings around them.

choices.text: Suspect acute angle-closure glaucoma and get intraocular pressure measured now
choices.feedback: Right. Mid-dilated fixed pupil, hazy cornea, halos, vomiting and a dark-theater trigger are the classic set. Pressure confirms it.

choices.text: Suspect anterior uveitis and start steroid drops
choices.feedback: Uveitis gives a small sluggish pupil, not a mid-dilated one, and treating blind here delays the pressure check that matters.

choices.text: Suspect optic neuritis and order an MRI
choices.feedback: Optic neuritis is painful with movement in a younger patient with an RAPD, not with a hazy cornea and halos. Imaging first wastes the window.

choices.text: Dilate the right pupil to get a good fundus view
choices.feedback: Dangerous. A dilating drop can slam the drainage angle completely shut and spike the pressure further.

steps.prompt: Right intraocular pressure is 58 mmHg. Left is 15 mmHg. She is still retching. Ophthalmology is 25 minutes away.

choices.text: Notify ophthalmology immediately, begin pressure-lowering therapy per protocol, and keep her in a lit room supine
choices.feedback: Correct. Every 10 minutes of pressure in the 50s costs retinal ganglion cells. Supine positioning and light both help the lens-iris relationship.

choices.text: Give an antiemetic and analgesia while waiting for ophthalmology to arrive
choices.feedback: Reasonable supportive care but not sufficient on its own. Pressure reduction should start now, not on arrival of the consultant.

choices.text: Place her in a dark quiet room to reduce photophobia while you wait
choices.feedback: Harmful. Darkness dilates the pupil further and worsens the angle block. Keep the room lit.

choices.text: Order a head CT to exclude an intracranial cause of the headache and vomiting
choices.feedback: The diagnosis is already made at the bedside with a pressure of 58. Imaging delays sight-saving treatment.

steps.prompt: Forty minutes later the pressure is 28 mmHg and her pain has eased. Ophthalmology is at the bedside planning a laser iridotomy. She asks whether her other eye is at risk.

choices.text: Explain that the fellow eye shares the same narrow anatomy and is usually treated preventively
choices.feedback: Correct. Prophylactic laser iridotomy of the unaffected eye is standard because the anatomic risk is bilateral.

choices.text: Tell her the other eye is unaffected and needs no attention
choices.feedback: Incorrect and falsely reassuring. Angle closure reflects anatomy, and the fellow eye carries substantial risk.

choices.text: Say you will let the ophthalmologist answer that specific question
choices.feedback: Safe but a missed teaching moment. You can share the general principle and let the specialist confirm the plan.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern: severe eye pain with nausea and vomiting, halos, a hazy cornea and a mid-dilated poorly reactive pupil after time in dim light. That combination is acute angle-closure glaucoma, and the confirming test is a pressure that often runs 40-70 mmHg. Two traps repeat on exams and on shift. First, the vomiting sends people down a headache or abdominal pathway and the eye never gets examined. Second, dilating drops and dark rooms both feel helpful and both make angle closure worse. Remember that acuity and pupils take ninety seconds and separate surface disease from an emergency, and that the fellow eye gets treated too.

scenarios.title: Working through a sore throat with a fever
scenarios.intro: You are given three patients with sore throats to reason through. Each one tests a different decision point: whether to test for strep, when a sore throat is actually an airway problem, and which antibiotic choices cause harm. Work them in order and commit to an answer before reading the feedback.

steps.prompt: Patient one is a 28-year-old with a 2-day sore throat, measured fever of 38.4 C, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes, and a dry cough. How do you score and act?

choices.text: Centor 3 with age modifier 0; the cough removes a point, so test with a rapid antigen test and treat only if positive
choices.feedback: Correct. Fever, exudate and tender nodes give 3; cough is present so the no-cough point is not earned. A score of 2-3 means test, then treat on the result.

choices.text: Centor 4; treat empirically with penicillin for 10 days without testing
choices.feedback: Overcounted. Cough is present, so that criterion scores zero. Empiric treatment at this score overtreats a likely viral illness.

choices.text: Centor 0; no testing and no antibiotics
choices.feedback: Undercounted. Fever, exudate and tender nodes are each real points. Skipping testing here can miss a treatable strep infection.

choices.text: Skip scoring entirely and give azithromycin because she is uncomfortable
choices.feedback: Harmful. Antibiotics without indication drive resistance and side effects, and macrolides are not first-line even when strep is confirmed.

steps.prompt: Patient two is a 19-year-old college student with 10 days of fatigue, sore throat with heavy exudate, fever, and tender nodes in the back of the neck. Spleen tip is palpable. What is the leading diagnosis and the key counseling point?

choices.text: Infectious mononucleosis; avoid contact sports and heavy lifting for at least 3-4 weeks
choices.feedback: Correct. Posterior cervical nodes, prolonged fatigue and splenomegaly point to EBV. Splenic rupture is rare but catastrophic, so activity restriction is the counseling that matters.

choices.text: Strep pharyngitis; start amoxicillin for 10 days
choices.feedback: This is the classic error. Posterior nodes and a 10-day course of fatigue fit EBV, and aminopenicillins produce a widespread rash in a large minority of mono patients.

choices.text: Viral pharyngitis; supportive care with no restrictions
choices.feedback: Half right. It is viral, but calling it a simple cold misses the enlarged spleen and the activity restriction that prevents rupture.

choices.text: Peritonsillar abscess; arrange drainage
choices.feedback: Wrong pattern. An abscess is unilateral with trismus, a muffled voice and uvular deviation, not bilateral exudate with posterior nodes and fatigue.

steps.prompt: Patient three is a 44-year-old with 8 hours of rapidly worsening throat pain. He is drooling into a cup, his voice is muffled, he sits leaning forward on his hands, and his oropharynx looks nearly normal. What is the first priority?

choices.text: Depress the tongue and swab for strep to complete the workup
choices.feedback: Dangerous. Instrumenting the oropharynx in suspected epiglottitis can trigger laryngospasm and complete obstruction.

choices.text: Keep him upright, give oxygen, and bring in personnel who can secure a difficult airway
choices.feedback: Correct. Drooling, muffled voice, tripod posture and a normal-looking throat point above the visible pharynx. Airway readiness comes before diagnosis.

choices.text: Lay him flat for a thorough head-to-toe examination
choices.feedback: Harmful. Supine positioning can close a swollen airway. He is sitting forward because that posture is keeping him breathing.

choices.text: Send him alone to radiology for a lateral neck film
choices.feedback: Unsafe. A thumbprint sign would support the diagnosis, but an unaccompanied trip risks obstruction away from help.

steps.prompt: Pulling the three cases together: what single feature most reliably separates a sore throat that needs a score and a swab from one that needs an airway team?

choices.text: The height of the fever
choices.feedback: Fever tracks infection severity poorly and does not distinguish a pharyngitis from an airway threat. Plenty of epiglottitis patients are only mildly febrile early.

choices.text: Whether the tonsils have visible exudate
choices.feedback: Exudate is a Centor criterion, but the most dangerous throats often look normal because the problem sits above or behind what you can see.

choices.text: Drooling with a muffled voice and a patient who will not lie down
choices.feedback: Correct. Pooling secretions, voice change and refusal to recline mean the airway is threatened, regardless of what the pharynx looks like.

choices.text: Whether the patient reports a cough
choices.feedback: Cough helps sort viral from streptococcal pharyngitis, but it says nothing about airway compromise.

scenarios.debrief: Three lessons stack here. First, Centor and McIsaac are arithmetic, not intuition: count fever, absent cough, exudate and tender anterior nodes, then adjust for age, and let 0-1 go untested, 2-3 get tested, and 4-5 get tested with reasonable empiric treatment. Second, the sore throat with weeks of fatigue, posterior nodes and a palpable spleen is mononucleosis, where aminopenicillins cause a rash and contact sports stop for 3-4 weeks. Third, none of the scoring matters if the patient is drooling, muffled and sitting forward. That triad moves the problem from the tonsils to the airway, and nothing goes in that mouth until someone who can secure an airway is standing there.
